tldr: The paper introduces Agent-as-a-Judge, a framework where agentic systems evaluate other agentic systems, providing rich intermediate feedback throughout task-solving trajectories, and a new benchmark called DevAI with 55 realistic AI development tasks.
contributions: Agent-as-a-Judge framework using agentic systems to evaluate agentic systems with intermediate feedback
DevAI benchmark with 55 real-world AI development tasks containing 365 hierarchical requirements and 125 preferences
Demonstration that Agent-as-a-Judge aligns with human evaluation at 90%, outperforming LLM-as-a-Judge at 70%
methods: The authors designed an Agent-as-a-Judge system with eight modular components (graph, locate, read, search, retrieve, ask, memory, and planning) that evaluate agentic system outputs against hierarchical requirements structured as a directed acyclic graph. They tested three open-source agentic frameworks (MetaGPT, GPT-Pilot, OpenHands) on 55 tasks from DevAI using a time limit of 1800 seconds per task with gpt-4o as the backend model. Three human evaluators performed manual assessments across two rounds including a consensus debate phase.
results: GPT-Pilot and OpenHands each satisfied approximately 29% of task requirements but only completed one full task entirely. Agent-as-a-Judge achieved 88.52%-92.07% alignment with human judges across models, significantly outperforming LLM-as-a-Judge at 65.30%-71.85%. The human evaluator disagreement rate ranged from 10%-30%, and majority voting reduced error rates to 6.01% from individual errors as high as 23.77%.
limitations: Human evaluation is prohibitively expensive requiring approximately 86.5 total human hours across two rounds. Single human evaluators show high disagreement (10-30%) and inconsistency. The planning and memory modules in Agent-as-a-Judge were found unstable and potentially detrimental due to error propagation from historical judgments.
